extracted.intended_audience: employers, safety professionals, small entity representatives, and stakeholders commenting on OSHA's proposed Heat Injury and Illness Prevention standard (NPRM)
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory preamble and options analysis for OSHA's proposed Heat Injury and Illness Prevention Program (HIIPP) standard, including alternatives, cost estimates, SBAR Panel recommendations, and OSHA responses to stakeholder concerns. Intended to inform rule design and solicit public comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify duplicative/overlapping/conflicting Federal rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the RFA, identify, 'to the extent practicable, . . . all relevant Federal rules which may duplicate, overlap or conflict with the proposed rule' (5 U.S.C. 603(b)(5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA discusses other Federal rules (EPA WPS, DOT/FMCSA, and existing OSHA standards) to determine duplication, overlap, or conflict and concluded it did not identify any rules that would conflict with the proposed standard. If specific requirements directly overlap, the specific requirements would apply in lieu of more general requirements (see 29 CFR 1910.5(c)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with EPA Worker Protection Standard (WPS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that EPA's WPS contains some provisions addressing heat hazards tied to PPE and training for pesticide handlers (40 CFR part 170).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although there may be overlap (e.g., training, PPE considerations), OSHA believes the proposed standard is consistent with WPS requirements and that WPS does not obviate the need for an OSHA heat standard designed specifically to protect workers from hazardous heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of DOT/FMCSA regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for DOT/FMCSA regulations that require instruction about extreme driving conditions, including high heat, for certain commercial drivers (49 CFR part 380).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These DOT requirements might overlap to the extent they require some training for a limited group, but they do not conflict with or obviate the comprehensive OSHA standard covering a broad range of workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship to existing OSHA sanitation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing sanitation standards (29 CFR 1910.141, 1926.51, 1915.88, 1917.127, 1918.95, 1928.110) require employers to provide readily accessible potable drinking water and toilet facilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These standards do not include the same level of specificity (e.g., specific quantity of water) as the proposed heat standard; they are complementary and do not obviate the need for heat-specific requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementarity with pipe-guarding standards in mills
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for pulp, paper, and textile mills require guarding of exposed hot water/steam pipes to prevent contact (29 CFR 1910.261(k)(11), 1910.262).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those provisions are primarily burn/scald protections but can be complementary to heat injury prevention if insulation reduces workplace temperatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping standard should not be duplicated
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's Recordkeeping standard (29 CFR 1904.7) requires recording/reporting of injuries and illnesses that meet recording criteria, including heat-related ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed heat standard does not add further injury/illness reporting requirements beyond 29 CFR 1904.7. Proposed recordkeeping is limited and targeted (see indoor monitoring records).

rubrics_metrics.name: Training standard differences and need for heat-specific training
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's Safety Training and Education standard for construction (29 CFR 1926.21) requires training on recognition/avoidance of unsafe conditions but does not specifically identify hazardous heat or establish heat-specific training requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A heat-specific standard should establish explicit training requirements because general training standards may not sufficiently address hazardous heat recognition, prevention, and response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory alternatives analysis per OMB Circular A-4
rubrics_metrics.description: For key attributes of the proposed standard, examine options including: the proposed option; at least one option achieving additional benefits (more stringent); and at least one option costing less (less stringent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA used this framework to analyze rest breaks and written HIIPPs as key provisions and presented alternatives and regulatory options (with cost comparisons) to solicit comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key attributes for analysis: rest breaks and written HIIPPs
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify rest break requirements and written Heat Injury and Illness Prevention Programs (HIIPPs) as central provisions for evaluating alternatives and impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA analyzes how changes to these attributes (frequency/duration of breaks; thresholds for written plans) affect protective benefits and compliance costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written HIIPP scope threshold (employer size)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed rule: establishments with 10 or more employees must have a written HIIPP; smaller employers must have a program but need not have it in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatives considered include requiring written HIIPPs for all establishments regardless of size (adds cost) or raising the threshold so establishments with <20 employees need not write a HIIPP (reduces cost). OSHA's rationale: smallest employers may communicate informally; written plans provide safety benefits for larger employers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of HIIPP review
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed: review HIIPP at least annually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative considered: review at least every other year (reduces cost but OSHA believes annual review is necessary to promptly identify and remedy deficiencies and align with other OSHA standards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Refresher training frequency for at-risk employees and designated persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed: annual refresher training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative: refresher training every other year (would reduce costs but OSHA preliminarily determined annual training is necessary to maintain requisite knowledge, particularly for outdoor workers before each heat season).

rubrics_metrics.name: High heat trigger level
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed high heat trigger: heat index of 90 °F (initial and high triggers discussed elsewhere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative considered: 95 °F high heat trigger (reduces costs but OSHA preliminarily determined 90 °F is more protective and that higher triggers such as NWS heat advisories may not be protective enough). OSHA provided methodology and evidence in Section V.B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rest break frequency and duration at high heat trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed: at or above the high heat trigger, provide a 15-minute paid rest break at least every two hours. No work activities allowed during these rest breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory options include 15-minute breaks at least every hour (much higher cost) and 10-minute breaks every two hours (lower cost). OSHA's literature basis supports 15-minute breaks every two hours at the high heat trigger, with access to shade, water, and ability to shed PPE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rest breaks at initial trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed: rest breaks at the initial heat trigger are required only when needed to prevent overheating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisions specify requirements for indoor and outdoor break areas and provide employer flexibility in cooling method selection; a meal break may count as a rest break under certain circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where rest breaks may occur and break area cooling options
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify acceptable break area types and cooling methods for indoor and outdoor breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options allowed include: for outdoor break areas, shade OR air conditioning; for indoor break areas, air conditioning OR increased air movement and, if appropriate, de-humidification. OSHA provides flexibility to employers to determine what works best for their employees and situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of permissible activities during rest breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: No work activities are allowed during rest breaks at the high heat trigger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA clarifies that rest breaks are periods for cooling and hydration, and the proposed summary/explanation specifies that no work activities would be allowed during these rest breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility in monitoring methods and heat metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow employers flexibility in what heat metric they use and how they measure heat in the workplace or worksite (e.g., forecast, on-site measurements, WBGT, heat index, apps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA permits outdoor employers to use forecasts instead of on-site monitoring and provides guidance on how and when monitoring must occur; Panel recommended not mandating a single measurement method due to variability across worksites and mobile workforces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indoor on-site temperature monitoring recordkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers of indoor workplaces are required to create written or electronic records of on-site temperature measurements and retain these records for a minimum of six months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers have flexibility: use monitoring devices with storage capability or create and maintain written records based on devices without digital recording. OSHA determined this aids in identifying workplace conditions and trends affecting employee health and safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement to document rest breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA is not requiring documentation of rest breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decision responds to stakeholder concerns that documenting rest breaks is infeasible or burdensome. OSHA determined recordkeeping will be limited (e.g., indoor monitoring data) and that rest break documentation is not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: No additional injury/illness reporting beyond existing recordkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed standard does not add injury/illness reporting requirements beyond 29 CFR 1904.7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA considered stakeholder concerns about requiring records of first-aid-only heat-related incidents and is not proposing to require additional reporting beyond existing rules; the only proposed recordkeeping requirement applies to indoor monitoring data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical surveillance optional alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory option to require medical screening questionnaires for all at-risk employees and medical examinations for those screened as predisposed to heat-related health risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA modeled this option with assumptions (questionnaire 15 minutes; 23% screened positive; medical exam one hour plus employer-paid exam cost of $501.28). This option would substantially increase costs (estimated +$2.5 billion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acclimatization period for returning employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed: acclimatization required for employees returning after 14 consecutive days away from work; alternative considered: 30 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing to 30 days reduces the estimated cost slightly; OSHA proposed the more protective 14-day approach given uncertainty in data and preliminary determinations about protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of sedentary work exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Define upper bound for sedentary work exemption with respect to indoor work areas and heat index thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative considered restricting the sedentary work exemption to sedentary activities at indoor work areas below a heat index of 90 °F, which would increase the number of employees qualifying for high heat-trigger protections and raise costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow performance-based provisions and multiple compliance methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel recommended, and OSHA drafted, performance-based provisions that allow employers to tailor HIIPPs to their workplace, including offering multiple methods of compliance where practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the proposed standard: exclusions for consistently air-conditioned indoor workplaces below 80°F, written-plan size threshold, employer choice of heat metric, and other determinations based on operations; OSHA requests comment on flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer flexibility for mobile workforces and variable indoor conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize challenges of monitoring for mobile workers and indoor temperature variability and allow tailored monitoring approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel and stakeholders reported measurement difficulties (site variability, mobile workers); OSHA provides guidance and flexibility particularly for outdoor forecast use and multiple monitoring options for employers with variable worksites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of various monitoring tools and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers may rely on a range of monitoring methods (OSHA/NIOSH Heat Safety Tool App, local weather forecasts, NWS calculators, thermometers, heat index monitors, wet bulb globe thermometers, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some stakeholders find certain metrics (WBGT, wet/dry bulb) confusing or burdensome; OSHA's approach is to allow methods that are appropriate and feasible for the employer while providing guidance on measurement and timing.
